In response to the incident, the Bulgarian Foreign Ministry has summoned Ukrainian Ambassador Olesya Ilashchuk for an explanation on Monday, Aug. 10. Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi stressed that Ukraine did not intentionally target Bulgaria and is fully cooperating with the investigation. He emphasized that the root cause of such regional security incidents remains Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine. The drone had entered Bulgarian airspace from Romania, flying low enough to evade air defense systems, and detonated in a field about one kilometer from a Trans-Balkan gas pipeline compressor station. by Kyiv Post | Aug. 9, 2026, 11:14 am Flip Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied A Bulgarian military police car is parked at an access to a farmland area where a drone that entered Bulgaria exploded, near the Kardam border-crossing between Bulgaria and Romania, Aug. 8, 2026. (Photo by Mihail IVANOV / AFP) Content Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Flip The Bulgarian Defense Ministry has identified the drone that exploded on Aug. 8 near the Kardam border crossing as a Ukrainian “Maiia” decoy drone, noting there is no evidence to suggest the crash was an intentional act. Following a preliminary analysis of the wreckage found near General Toshevo, the Defense Ministry stated that this specific type of decoy drone is widely used by the Ukrainian military. JOIN US ON TELEGRAM Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official . Despite the assessment that the crash was accidental, the incident has triggered a diplomatic response. According to BNT News , the Bulgarian Foreign Ministry announced that Foreign Minister Velislava Petrova has summoned the Ukrainian Ambassador to Bulgaria, Olesya Ilashchuk, to provide an explanation. The meeting is scheduled for Monday, Aug. 10, as the ambassador is currently out of the country. Advertisement Ukraine responds to the drone incident Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi quickly addressed the situation, assuring that Kyiv is in close contact with Bulgarian authorities to clarify the circumstances of the crash. “We can definitely say that the Ukrainian Defense Forces did not intentionally direct any assets toward Bulgaria. We are currently clarifying all the circumstances of what happened and all the technical facts,” Tykhyi told reporters. “We are completely open to cooperating with Bulgaria to clarify the details.” Tykhyi also reminded the international community of the broader context, pointing out that the root cause of such incidents remains the ongoing war initiated by Russia. Other Topics of Interest Ukraine Buys 70 ATACMS Missiles From Turkey The US State Department has notified Congress of a massive arms transfer from Turkey to Ukraine, including 70 ATACMS missiles and 12 M270 MLRS launchers. “It is important to note that the root cause of all incidents of this type is Russia’s war against Ukraine , which has been going on for five years, is being purposefully prolonged by Moscow , and threatens not only Ukrainians but also, unfortunately, other peoples and countries,” Tykhyi stated. “That is why an early end to the war is critical to ensuring the security of the region, and we count on working together with our partners to force Moscow to make peace.” Advertisement Drone crash in Bulgaria The diplomatic fallout follows a Saturday morning incident where a drone crossed from Romania into Bulgarian airspace and exploded in a sunflower field about 100 meters inside the border . Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev confirmed that there were no casualties or damage to infrastructure, though the device detonated just one kilometer away from a compressor station for the Trans-Balkan gas pipeline. Following an emergency meeting of Bulgaria’s Security Council, Radev explained that the drone had evaded both Romanian and Bulgarian air defense systems due to its low altitude, making it impossible to ensure dense radar coverage. In response to the incursion, Radev announced that Bulgaria would redeploy border guard personnel and anti-drone equipment from its border with Turkey to the Romanian border to better monitor the area. https://www.politico.eu/article/pressure.text: Europe is facing increasing pressure to create a more favorable market for the life sciences sector as the Trump administration continues its push for drugmakers to invest in the U.S. Washington announced nine more deals with pharmaceutical companies to lower certain drug prices on Monday evening, bringing to 26 the total number of agreements. These so-called most-favored-nation deals aim to compel companies to launch new medicines in the United States at prices similar to those in Europe, while avoiding some tariffs. They also commit firms to invest in new facilities in America, with at least $19.6 billion pledged so far, the White House said. Advertisement Advertisement Industry leaders in Europe warn that if the U.S. continues to sign more deals with companies — designed to drive down prices for American citizens while boosting U.S. investments — European patients will feel the effects. Since the most-favored nation policy will see Washington copy some EU countries’ prices, companies are opting not to launch new drugs in Europe to maintain higher prices in the U.S. where they can make bigger profits. In addition, companies are increasingly choosing America for research and manufacturing. “Companies may hesitate to launch in Europe or in Japan or Canada if they think that the price in Europe or Japan or Canada will be lower than the price they could obtain in the U.S.,” Adrian van den Hoven, director general of Medicines for Europe, told POLITICO. “That's the risk for Europe going forward.” Medicines for Europe represents the generics industry, which largely makes cheaper off-patent medicines. Two large generics firms that also make branded drugs were included in the nine new deals. Meanwhile, Europe’s current biggest offering to entice industry to stay local — a proposed patent extension for certain biotech drugs — is too little too late, some argue. Industry says the patent extension comes with too many conditions and it won’t come into effect in time to stop the sector from pivoting more to America where market conditions are more favorable. The patent extension and other industry perks in the proposed Biotech Act are a step in the right direction, said Alexander Natz, secretary general of the European Confederation of Pharmaceutical Entrepreneurs. But “it’s probably too late if we wait for the Biotech Act” to take effect, likely in a couple of years, he said. Capturing more companies The latest deals mark a shift away from the previous 17 deals with multi-billion dollar big pharmaceutical companies and include a mix from small specialist firms with only a handful of licensed drugs to vast generic drugmakers. Advertisement Advertisement The new agreements show that the most-favored-nation policy “has entered a new phase, now explicitly involving mid-sized pharmaceutical companies,” Natz said. EUCOPE represents small and mid-sized biotech and pharma companies. The deals link drug pricing with trade and manufacturing commitments, he said. “For Europe, the implications therefore go well beyond individual medicine prices. They potentially affect patient access, launch and investment decisions, and ultimately where innovation and manufacturing take place,” Natz said. “As the U.S. approach continues to evolve, Europe needs to follow these developments closely and maintain an active dialogue with industry.” Over to EU Drug pricing decisions in Europe are taken nationally as opposed to by the EU. Nonetheless, the European Commission controls many of the market conditions for the sector, from patent durations to clinical trials regulations and marketing authorizations. Eva Hrncirova, a spokesperson for the European Commission, said Tuesday that they “closely monitor the implementation of the U.S. most-favored-nation policy and any potential effects on the European market.” Advertisement Advertisement “Our priority is obviously to ensure that patients get timely access to safe, effective and affordable medicines.” A European Commission analysis — done at the request of EU health ministers — states that it is too early to tell what effect U.S. President Donald Trump’s drug pricing policies will have on medicine launches and prices in Europe. Diederik Stadig, a health care economist at Dutch bank ING, however said there have already been fewer drug launch applications to the European Medicines Agency in the first four months of 2026. “The initial picture is [fewer] launches in Europe, and still high prices in the United States. So for American patients, the upside to these policies is very limited,” he said. EU vs. the capitals Trump wants European countries to pay more for drugs, arguing the U.S. subsidizes lower drug prices in Europe. Only the U.K. has agreed to pay more for medicines . Faced with the growing pressure from the U.S. and pharma companies, the EU and countries are increasingly working together to show a united front in maintaining strict price controls. Some are urging fellow member countries not to fall into the temptation of bilateral deals like the U.K. Advertisement Advertisement But drug pricing is only part of the equation, Stadig said. “If Europe were to double its medicine prices, that would do little for the attractiveness of Europe because Europe faces a fundamental issue that’s different than just price.” Europe struggles with a fragmented drug pricing model and has a big “commercialization gap,” Stadig said, where world-leading science in Europe eventually leads to market launches outside of the bloc. For Nathalie Moll, director general of the European Federation of Pharmaceutical Industries and Associations, it’s European countries that need to invest in making the bloc more attractive. “Europe’s ability to safeguard patient access to innovative medicines is closely linked to market conditions and its wider trade, industrial and competitiveness policies,” she said, calling on EU governments to invest in market reforms. But there doesn’t seem enough urgency to act, Stadig added. Advertisement Advertisement “As far as that goes, I’m seeing endless discussions and very little happening,” Stadig said. “The European Commission has diagnosed the issue, laying out potential solutions in legislations like the pharmaceutical package, the Biotech Act, and the Critical Medicines Act,” Stadig said. “They're doing what they can … I think national governments are the issue in this case.”

Speaking not in Saxony-Anhalt but in the neighboring state of Lower Saxony , Merz said "we must engage more effectively with this party." "We must address the issues at hand," he said. "We must also address our choice of words." Merz also referenced recent comments by AfD's state leader in Saxony-Anhalt, Martin Reichardt, who said the modern German state had become "a lazy, anti-social bum reeking of dope." The chancellor said such comments show "what these people think of our country." "We will not let these people talk our country down," he added. Merz said that "Germany can look back on a success story spanning almost 80 years, albeit with many problems and many challenges." "But we are still one of the most prosperous countries in the world," he said. "We are still one of the safest countries in the world. And we are still a stable, well-established democracy." Merz remains unpopular nationally. In a Trendbarometer survey published by broadcaster RTL earlier this week, just 14% of respondents said they were satisfied with the chancellor's work. He has kept a relatively low profile in Saxony-Anhalt during the state election campaign. In recent days, he made two visits to the towns of Quedlinburg and Leuna where he held closed-door meetings with candidates from his party, the Christian Democratic Union (CDU). https://p.dw.com/p/5LgEP Skip next section Thousands turn out at 'Democracy Festival' in Saxony-Anhalt 09/05/2026 September 5, 2026 Thousands turn out at 'Democracy Festival' in Saxony-Anhalt Police estimated that 6,000 people turned out at the demo in Magdeburg Image: Jan Woitas/dpa/picture alliance Thousands of people joined a "march for democracy" on Saturday in Magdeburg , the capital of Saxony-Anhalt . Organized by a coalition called "Saxony-Anhalt: Open to the World," the march was called to uphold values of democracy, diversity and inclusivity ahead of a state election in which the far-right Alternative for Germany party (AfD) is comfortably leading opinion polls. Germany's federal intelligence service has labeled the AfD state branch in Saxony-Anhalt as a right-wing extremist organization. At the demo on Saturday, attendees carried signs that read "more love, less hate," "a better life without Nazis," and "the potato is also of foreign origin," among other slogans. Signs included slogans such as: 'A better life without Nazis' Image: Jan Woitas/dpa/picture alliance Police estimated that some 6,000 people participated in the march from Magdeburg's central station to Cathedral Square, where another 3,000 people joined them. Among them were contingents from trade unions, church groups and other civic organizations. "As initiatives, clubs, associations, and individuals, we are taking a stand and advocating for respectful coexistence in our state," the organizers stated in their call to action. According to police, eight gatherings had been registered to take place in Magdeburg on Saturday. Others included a human chain for democracy and a democracy-themed cycling tour. In an interview with German daily the Tagesspiegel , right-wing extremism expert Heike Kleffner praised the organizers' "paradoxical confidence" in being able to mobilize democratic masses despite being under attack. The demonstrators marched to Magdeburg's Cathedral Square Image: Jan Woitas/dpa/picture alliance https://p.dw.com/p/5LgCM Skip next section Steinmeier urges unity ahead of Saxony-Anhalt election 09/05/2026 September 5, 2026 Steinmeier urges unity ahead of Saxony-Anhalt election Steinmeier attended a community event in Bonn, western Germany, on Friday Image: Marc John/Bonn.digital/picture alliance President Frank-Walter Steinmeier has warned that Germany's democracy and rule of law need protection from those "who scorn and trample all over them." Steinmeier was speaking ahead of Sunday's state election in Saxony-Anhalt , where the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is expected to receive by far the most votes. While not singling out any party, he appeared to take aim at AfD's policies and rhetoric, which critics describe as extremist and anti-migrant and supporters label a patriotic defense of national borders and security. "Ethnic-based thinking and nationalist isolationism are simply not the answer to the challenges of the 21st century," Steinmeier told a community festival in Bonn. Steinmeier, who steps down from office in March after ten years, described liberal democracy as an "achievement" and "a blessing for us all." He said those who wish to protect and preserve democracy represent the majority and that anger and outrage offer no way forward. "You cannot build a future on hatred and incitement," Steinmeier warned. The most serious incident was on Tuesday evening at a substation in Bergheim, west of Cologne. Launch devices were used to fire cables across overhead lines, causing a short circuit that forced five units of the nearby Niederaussem coal plant to temporarily disconnect from the network. Earlier the same day, a similar attack was carried out near the Jänschwalde plant in eastern Brandenburg. More than a dozen launch devices were found. On Thursday, a passer-by found similar unused devices at a substation in Dormagen, between Cologne and Düsseldorf. Police say the objects matched the launch gear used in the other incidents. Sabotage fears hit Germany's power grid To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Germany's DPA news agency reported on Friday that a man from a town near Dortmund claimed responsibility for the incidents in two letters. His motive is reportedly to draw attention to the use of fossil fuels in electricity production, which he called a "crime." This week, officers found explosives in the 48-year-old's home, while a special operations unit stormed a truck in a wood, some 100 kilometers (62 miles) away. The suspect was not found. The FBI is prepared to pay up to $150,000 for any information about his whereabouts. https://p.dw.com/p/5LekM Skip next section Four states demand federal support to waterways after drought 09/05/2026 September 5, 2026 Four states demand federal support to waterways after drought Water levels on the Rhine River reached record lows at times this summer Image: Hesham Elsherif/Anadolu/picture alliance After a summer drought caused severe low water levels on the Rhine River , four of Germany's states have called on Berlin to increase funding to modernize inland waterways. Hesse, Rhineland-Palatinate, Baden-Württemberg and North Rhine-Westphalia said the federal government must invest at least €2.5 billion ($2.9 billion) per year to boost maintenance. Germany's waterways, including the Rhine, play a key role in moving raw materials across the country, carrying more than 5% of all freight transported, They said politicians often focus on investing in roads and railways, while canals and rivers often get neglected. Over the summer, the Rhine became almost impassable at one key location and many ships plying the Rhine had to operate with much-reduced cargoes. Economists at the Kiel Institute for the World Economy estimated the drought would cause an economic loss of up to €2 billion. North Rhine-Westphalia's Transport Minister Viktor Haase called for new fleets of inland vessels that can reliably operate even in extreme low-water conditions. https://p.dw.com/p/5Ledd Skip next section Several rallies planned on eve of Saxony-Anhalt state election 09/05/2026 September 5, 2026 Several rallies planned on eve of Saxony-Anhalt state election Saxony-Anhalt holds its state election on Sunday Image: Peter Gercke/dpa/picture alliance Thousands of people are expected at rallies in eastern Germany's state of Saxony-Anhalt ahead of elections for a new regional parliament. Police said 12 events have been registered in the state capital, Magdeburg, with others in Halle. Most of the demonstrations are against the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, which is widely expected to receive the most support in Sunday's vote. Trade unions and civil society groups are organizing the largest rallies. Their events include a so-called democracy festival. The AfD will also hold its final campaign event in Magdeburg. The latest polls put the AfD at over 40% support, putting it on course to be the largest party in the state parliament by a wide margin. However, without an outright majority, the chance of the AfD forming a government will get messy as mainstream parties have ruled out a coalition with the far right. No smaller party expected to enter parliament has offered to formally support an AfD-led government. The AfD could take office on its own only if it wins a majority of seats. https://p.dw.com/p/5LeNR Skip next section Welcome to our coverage 09/05/2026 September 5, 2026 Welcome to our coverage Wesley Dockery Editor Guten Morgen from Germany , where more than a dozen rallies are planned ahead of Sunday's state election in Saxony-Anhalt. https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/13/euro.text: Poland’s Minister of National Defence and Deputy Prime Minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, said Europe must adopt a “war-mode” mentality in its defence sector or risk harming Europeans in the future.“I am actually an advocate for the war-mode when it comes to the production in defence sector,” he said at a press conference on the sidelines of the Warsaw Security Forum on Tuesday.“This is what the Russian Federation does at the moment. We cannot overlook this fact.”Russia shifted towards wartime defence production before its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and is projected to spend 7.5% of its gross domestic product on its armed forces in 2026.In 2025, Russia produced roughly seven million artillery, mortar, tank and rocket rounds, according to a recent Estonian intelligence report. Russian forces currently use roughly 10,000 to 15,000 rounds per day in their continued aggression against Ukraine.In contrast, Europe’s defence industry has been shaped by decades of underinvestment and fragmentation.Russia is outpacing the EU in ammunition production, with the 27 member states and Norway expected to produce just two million 150mm ammunition shells this year, according to a leaked report on Europe’s defence readiness.Rearmament efforts by European countries and NATO members have driven the strongest annual increase in defence spending since the Cold War. Despite this, EU member states’ total defence spending in 2025 was estimated at €418 billion, or 2.2% of EU's total GDP, the report states.Kosiniak-Kamysz said the “time has come” for Europe to prepare to defend itself by multiplying its defence production.Failure to do so would be a “costly” mistake for Europeans, he warned, adding: “It's one of the disadvantages, but also it will impact (and) affect us negatively in future generations.”Poland is among the biggest spenders of its GDP on defence capabilities, spending 4.7% on core defence capabilities, according to the US envoy to NATO, Matthew Whitaker.
